resources.name: Instituto Cervantes, modelos de examen DELE
resources.why: The complete official sample papers for DELE A1, A2 and B1, free: the exam booklets as PDFs, the audio for the listening tasks, the transcripts, the answer keys and samples of graded writing and speaking. This is the exam itself rather than anyone's imitation of it, so do a full paper under real timing before you book a sitting. The mock exams in this app mirror these formats section by section.

resources.name: Diccionario de la lengua española (RAE)
resources.why: The dictionary the language is defined by, free online. Two things make it worth using over a bilingual app: it defines Spanish in Spanish, which is the habit that lifts you off translation, and every verb entry carries a full conjugation table, so it answers most of what you will actually want to look up while writing.

resources.name: Plan curricular del Instituto Cervantes
resources.why: The official syllabus for Spanish as a foreign language, level by level, from the same body that sets the DELE. Its grammar and vocabulary inventories are laid out in two columns so you can see exactly what belongs to your level and what belongs to the next one. This course's topic sequence is built against it.

resources.name: Aveteca del Centro Virtual Cervantes
resources.why: Free graded activities sorted by level, over a hundred of them across A1 to B1, each with a teacher sheet explaining the point. Good for a second pass on a grammar topic that did not land the first time, because the explanation comes from a different direction than this course's.

resources.name: Diccionario panhispánico de dudas (RAE)
resources.why: The reference for the questions a dictionary does not answer: which preposition a verb takes, whether an expression is standard, and how usage differs across the Spanish-speaking world. That last part matters here, because this course teaches the peninsular standard and this book will tell you calmly what the American alternative is without calling either one wrong.

resources.name: FundéuRAE, Fundación del Español Urgente
resources.why: Short daily notes on how to write current Spanish well: the word people are getting wrong this week, the accent that is disappearing, the borrowed English term and its Spanish equivalent. Two minutes a day, and it keeps your written register modern rather than textbook.

resources.name: Notes in Spanish
resources.why: Unscripted conversation recorded in Madrid, graded beginner to advanced, with a large free archive. It is the closest thing to overhearing real peninsular Spanish at a speed you can survive, which is exactly what the listening prueba tests and what a course alone cannot give you.

resources.name: News in Slow Spanish
resources.why: Current affairs read at a deliberately reduced speed with the transcript alongside. Use it as the bridge between classroom audio and real broadcast speed: listen once without the text, once with it, then once without again.

resources.name: Radio Ambulante
resources.why: Long-form narrative journalism from across Latin America, with transcripts. Included deliberately: the B1 exam draws its listening and reading texts from every variety of Spanish, not only the peninsular one, so training your ear on American accents is exam preparation and not a detour.

resources.name: RTVE Noticias
resources.why: Spanish news at full native speed, unadapted. Save it for the second half of the course and treat it as a stress test rather than a study tool: if you can follow the headlines and the first sentence of each story, your listening is where B1 needs it to be.
